<title>Wildlife of Antarctica</title>
<fragment>

Antarctica's cold deserts have some of the least diverse fauna in the world. Terrestrial vertebrates are limited to subantarctic islands, and even then they are limited in number.[12] Antarctica, including the subantarctic islands, has no natural fully terrestrial mammals, reptiles, or amphibians. Human activity has however led to the introduction in some areas of foreign species, such as rats, mice, chickens, rabbits, cats, pigs, sheep, cattle, reindeer, and various fish.[12] Invertebrates, such as beetle species, have also been introduced.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>

The four species that inhabit sea ice are thought to make up 50% of the total biomass of the world's seals.[28] Crabeater seals have a population of around 15 million, making them one of the most numerous large animals on the planet.[29] The New Zealand sea lion (*Phocarctos hookeri*), one of the rarest and most localised pinnipeds, breeds almost exclusively on the subantarctic Auckland Islands, although historically it had a wider range.[30] Out of all permanent mammalian residents, the Weddell seals live the furthest south.[31]


There are 10 cetacean species found in the Southern Ocean; six baleen whales, and four toothed whales. The largest of these, the blue whale (*Balaenoptera musculus*), grows to 24 metres (79 ft) long weighing 84 tonnes. Many of these species are migratory, and travel to tropical waters during the Antarctic winter.[32] Orcas, which do not migrate, nonetheless regularly travel to warmer waters, possibly to relieve the stress the temperature has on their skin.[33]

### Land invertebrates

[edit]

![](image)A pair of *Belgica antarctica*, the only insect on mainland Antarctica.
Most terrestrial invertebrates are restricted to the subantarctic islands. Although there are very few species, those that do inhabit Antarctica have high population densities. In the more extreme areas of the mainland, such as the cold deserts, food webs are sometimes restricted to three nematode species, only one of which is a predator.[12] Many invertebrates on the subantarctic islands can live in subzero temperatures without freezing, whereas those on the mainland can survive being frozen.[13]


Mites and springtails make up most terrestrial arthropod species, although various spiders, beetles, and flies can be found.[12] Several thousand individuals from various mite and springtail species can be found in 1 square metre (10.8 sq ft). Beetles and flies are the most species rich insect groups on the islands. Insects play an important role in recycling dead plant material.[13]


</fragment>
<fragment>
See also: Antarctic realm and Climate of Antarctica

![](image)Elevation of the Antarctic terrain
Around 98% of continental Antarctica is covered in ice up to 4.7 kilometres (2.9 mi) thick.[1] Antarctica's icy deserts have extremely low temperatures, high solar radiation, and extreme dryness.[2] Any precipitation that does fall usually falls as snow, and is restricted to a band around 300 kilometres (186 mi) from the coast. Some areas receive as little as 50 mm (2.0 in) of precipitation annually. The coldest temperature recorded on Earth was −89.4 °C (−128.9 °F) at Vostok Station on the Antarctic Plateau.[1] Organisms that survive in Antarctica are often extremophiles.[2]

The **Arabian Desert** (Template:Lang-ar) is a vast desert wilderness in West Asia that occupies almost the entire Arabian Peninsula with an area of 2,330,000 square kilometers (900,000 sq mi).[3] It stretches from Yemen to the Persian Gulf and Oman to Jordan and Iraq. It is the fifth largest desert in the world and the largest in Asia. At its center is *Ar-Rub' al-Khali* (The Empty Quarter), one of the largest continuous bodies of sand in the world. It is an extension of the Sahara Desert.[4]

Gazelles, oryx, sand cats, and spiny-tailed lizards are just some of the desert-adapted species that survive in this extreme environment, which features everything from red dunes to deadly quicksand. The climate is mostly dry (the major part receives around 100 mm (3.9 in) of rain per year, but some very rare places receive as little as 50 mm), and temperatures oscillate between very high heat and seasonal night time freezes. It is part of the deserts and xeric shrublands biome and lie in biogeographical realms of the Palearctic (northern part) and Afrotropical (southern part).


The Arabian Desert ecoregion has little biodiversity, although a few endemic plants grow here. Many species, such as the striped hyena, jackal and honey badger have died out as a result of hunting, habitat destruction, overgrazing by livestock, off-road driving, and human encroachment on their habitat. Other species, such as the Arabian sand gazelle, have been successfully re-introduced and are protected at reserves.

Threats to the ecoregion include overgrazing by livestock and feral camels and goats, wildlife poaching, and damage to vegetation by off-road driving.[2]

Based on my research from Wikipedia, here are the four largest deserts on Earth and the dominant types of animal life found in each:

## The Four Largest Deserts and Their Dominant Animal Life

### 1. **Antarctic Desert** (14,200,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Marine Mammals and Seabirds**
- The Antarctic is classified as a polar ice and tundra desert
- Dominant life consists of marine animals: seals (crabeater, Weddell, leopard, and fur seals) and whales (blue whales, orcas)
- Penguins are the primary seabirds, along with other flying birds like petrels and skuas
- Terrestrial life is extremely limited - mainly invertebrates like mites, springtails, and midges, including *Belgica antarctica* (the only insect on mainland Antarctica)

### 2. **Arctic Desert** (13,900,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Terrestrial Mammals**
- Arctic tundra desert with diverse cold-adapted mammals
- Dominant species include caribou/reindeer, Arctic foxes, Arctic hares, muskoxen, and polar bears (along coastal areas)
- Wolves, lemmings, and various bird species that migrate seasonally
- Marine life includes seals, walruses, and whales in Arctic waters

### 3. **Sahara Desert** (9,200,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Reptiles and Small Mammals**
- World's largest hot desert (subtropical)
- Dominated by reptiles: lizards (including monitor lizards), snakes (vipers, cobras), and chameleons
- Small mammals like gerbils, jerboas, fennec foxes, and desert hares
- Larger mammals include gazelles, addax antelope, and dromedary camels
- Insects and arachnids are abundant (scorpions, beetles)

### 4. **Great Australian Desert** (2,700,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Marsupials and Reptiles**
- Subtropical desert covering much of central Australia
- Dominated by marsupials: kangaroos, wallabies, and koalas in wooded areas
- Extensive reptile populations: numerous lizard species (including goannas), snakes, and turtles
- Unique Australian species like the thorny devil lizard
- Also hosts significant populations of feral camels (the largest in the world)
- Bird species include emus and various desert-adapted birds

## Summary
The animal life in each desert reflects the specific climate conditions - polar deserts support marine ecosystems, while hot deserts favor reptiles and small mammals, and the unique Australian desert hosts specialized marsupials that have adapted to arid conditions over millions of years.

Based on my research from Wikipedia, here are the four largest deserts on Earth and the dominant types of animal life found in each:

## The Four Largest Deserts and Their Dominant Animal Life

### 1. **Antarctic Desert** (14,200,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Marine Mammals and Seabirds**
- The Antarctic is classified as a polar ice and tundra desert
- Dominant life consists of marine animals: seals (crabeater, Weddell, leopard, and fur seals) and whales (blue whales, orcas)
- Penguins are the primary seabirds, along with other flying birds like petrels and skuas
- Terrestrial life is extremely limited - mainly invertebrates like mites, springtails, and midges, including *Belgica antarctica* (the only insect on mainland Antarctica)

### 2. **Arctic Desert** (13,900,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Terrestrial Mammals**
- Arctic tundra desert with diverse cold-adapted mammals
- Dominant species include caribou/reindeer, Arctic foxes, Arctic hares, muskoxen, and polar bears (along coastal areas)
- Wolves, lemmings, and various bird species that migrate seasonally
- Marine life includes seals, walruses, and whales in Arctic waters

### 3. **Sahara Desert** (9,200,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Reptiles and Small Mammals**
- World's largest hot desert (subtropical)
- Dominated by reptiles: lizards (including monitor lizards), snakes (vipers, cobras), and chameleons
- Small mammals like gerbils, jerboas, fennec foxes, and desert hares
- Larger mammals include gazelles, addax antelope, and dromedary camels
- Insects and arachnids are abundant (scorpions, beetles)

### 4. **Great Australian Desert** (2,700,000 km²)
**Dominant Animal Life: Marsupials and Reptiles**
- Subtropical desert covering much of central Australia
- Dominated by marsupials: kangaroos, wallabies, and koalas in wooded areas
- Extensive reptile populations: numerous lizard species (including goannas), snakes, and turtles
- Unique Australian species like the thorny devil lizard
- Also hosts significant populations of feral camels (the largest in the world)
- Bird species include emus and various desert-adapted birds

## Summary
The animal life in each desert reflects the specific climate conditions - polar deserts support marine ecosystems, while hot deserts favor reptiles and small mammals, and the unique Australian desert hosts specialized marsupials that have adapted to arid conditions over millions of years.
